blocks.content: Every running program constantly works with addresses: the address of a variable, the address a pointer holds, the address the next instruction sits at. It is tempting to assume these addresses point straight at physical RAM chips inside the machine, the same way a street address points at a real building. For almost every modern operating system that assumption is wrong, and understanding why is the single most important idea in this entire module.

This chapter opens the Memory Management module by drawing the line between the address a program sees and the address the hardware actually uses: what each one is, why the operating system deliberately keeps them apart, the Memory Management Unit that performs the translation, base and limit registers as the simplest relocation and protection mechanism, and when this translation actually happens.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759734-219294268.png
1. Two Different Addresses for the Same Byte
blocks.text: 1. Two Different Addresses for the Same Byte

blocks.content: A logical address, also called a virtual address, is the address a running program actually uses and sees. It is generated by the CPU while the program executes, built from whatever the program's own instructions reference: a variable's location, a function's entry point, an element inside an array. A physical address is something else entirely: it is the real, physical location inside the computer's RAM hardware, the actual memory cell that electrical signals reach.

These two addresses are not the same number, and in almost every modern system they are never the same number. A program can print out what looks like an address, ask for the value stored there, and receive correct data every time, all without that printed number ever matching the real physical location the data lives at.

Something in between is doing the translation quietly, on the program's behalf, without the program asking for it or even knowing it happened. That something is dedicated hardware, and it is the subject of this entire chapter.

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: A logical address is what the program sees and uses. A physical address is where the data actually lives in RAM. They are two different numbers connected by a translation step, not the same address seen twice.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759735-69373000.png
blocks.alt: Two Different Addresses for the Same Byte

blocks.content: 2. Why the Separation Exists

This separation is not an accident or a leftover of old hardware, it is a deliberate design choice that solves three real problems at once. The clearest way to see why is to imagine what would break if a program's addresses always had to match the real physical RAM locations exactly.

["The operating system can freely move a program to a different physical location in RAM whenever it needs to, without the program ever knowing or caring, because the program's own logical addresses never change.","Every program can be written and compiled as if it owns the entire address space starting at address zero, which massively simplifies compilers and linkers, since two different programs can both believe they start at zero without ever colliding in the real hardware.","This same separation is the foundation that makes virtual memory possible at all, letting a system run programs whose combined logical address spaces are far larger than the physical RAM actually installed, a full topic covered in its own dedicated chapter later in this module."]
items: The operating system can freely move a program to a different physical location in RAM whenever it needs to, without the program ever knowing or caring, because the program's own logical addresses never change.

Every program can be written and compiled as if it owns the entire address space starting at address zero, which massively simplifies compilers and linkers, since two different programs can both believe they start at zero without ever colliding in the real hardware.

This same separation is the foundation that makes virtual memory possible at all, letting a system run programs whose combined logical address spaces are far larger than the physical RAM actually installed, a full topic covered in its own dedicated chapter later in this module.

blocks.content: /engineering/library/os/images/1785408759735-313986000.png

Notice the pattern in all three benefits: the program stays completely unaware. It keeps issuing the same logical addresses it always would, and something else quietly makes sure those addresses land in the correct real location every time. That something else is dedicated hardware, introduced next.

blocks.title: Coming up next
blocks.content: Virtual memory takes this same logical versus physical split and pushes it further, letting programs use more address space than physically exists. That mechanism gets its own dedicated chapter later in this module.
3. The Memory Management Unit, the MMU
blocks.text: 3. The Memory Management Unit, the MMU

blocks.content: The Memory Management Unit, almost always shortened to MMU, is the hardware component that performs the actual translation from logical address to physical address. It usually sits directly on the CPU chip itself, positioned between the processor core and the memory bus, so that it can intercept every address before it ever reaches RAM.

The detail beginners most often miss is that this happens on every single memory access, not once at program startup and not just occasionally. Every instruction fetch, every variable read, every variable write, every stack push, generates a logical address, and every one of them is translated by the MMU in real time, transparently, before the actual RAM hardware is touched. The running program has no way to observe this happening; from its own point of view it simply reads and writes memory.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759735-379302875.png
blocks.alt: The Memory Management Unit, the MMU

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","What the MMU does"],"rows":[["1","Receives the logical address generated by the currently executing instruction"],["2","Checks that address against the limit register for the running program"],["3","Adds the base register value to produce the physical address"],["4","Sends the physical address onward to the memory bus and into RAM"]]}
Every memory reference a program makes is a logical address. It is the Memory Management Unit, not the program itself, that decides where that reference actually lands in RAM.
4. A Worked Example, Translating One Address
blocks.text: 4. A Worked Example, Translating One Address

blocks.content: The easiest way to make this concrete is to walk through one single translation with real numbers. Suppose a running program executes an instruction that reads a variable stored at logical address 1000. That is the number the program's own code actually contains and works with, nothing more exotic than that.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759735-555665940.png
blocks.alt: A Worked Example, Translating One Address

blocks.content: The MMU holds a base register value of 5000 for this particular program, meaning this program's block of physical memory begins at address 5000. The MMU simply adds the logical address to the base register: 1000 plus 5000 equals 6000. That 6000 is the physical address actually sent to the RAM chips, and the program never has to know that number even exists.
5. Base and Limit Registers, Relocation and Protection
blocks.text: 5. Base and Limit Registers, Relocation and Protection

blocks.content: The base register from the worked example is one half of the simplest possible relocation mechanism, and it is almost always paired with a second register called the limit register. The base register holds the starting physical address where this program's memory begins. The limit register holds the size of that program's address space, the maximum logical address it is allowed to use.

Every logical address must be checked against the limit register before any translation happens at all. If the logical address is smaller than the limit, the access is legal, and the MMU proceeds to add the base register exactly as shown in the worked example. If the logical address is equal to or greater than the limit, the access is illegal, and the hardware refuses to translate it at all.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759736-136214471.png
blocks.alt: Base and Limit Registers, Relocation and Protection

blocks.title: Protection, not just relocation
blocks.content: The base and limit register pair is also the operating system's most basic protection mechanism. Because every address is checked against the limit before translation, one program can never reach into another program's memory region, even by accident, since any attempt beyond its own limit is trapped by the hardware itself.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759736-716532839.png
blocks.alt: Base and Limit Registers, Relocation and Protection

blocks.content: This trap is a hardware level event, not something the misbehaving program can catch or ignore. Control passes immediately to the operating system, which typically ends the offending process with a memory access fault. This is exactly the mechanism that stops one buggy or malicious program from corrupting another program's data.
6. Two Programs, Two Relocations

The base and limit mechanism becomes even clearer once two programs run side by side. Each one is compiled and written as though its own logical address space starts at zero, completely unaware of the other program's existence. The operating system gives each one a different base register, and that single difference is enough to keep them apart in physical RAM.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759736-888170655.png

{"headers":["Program","Base register","Limit register","Logical address range it sees","Actual physical address range in RAM"],"rows":[["Program A","5000","2000","0 to 1999","5000 to 6999"],["Program B","8000","1500","0 to 1499","8000 to 9499"]]}

Program A's logical addresses 0 through 1999 land in physical addresses 5000 through 6999, while Program B's logical addresses 0 through 1499 land in physical addresses 8000 through 9499. Both programs are convinced they own the low end of memory starting at zero, and neither one can accidentally read or write the other's data, because each one's limit register stops it firmly at the edge of its own region.
7. When Translation Actually Happens

Address translation, sometimes called address binding, does not always happen at the same point in a program's lifetime. There are three distinct moments where a logical address can be bound to a physical address, and knowing all three by name matters for interviews as much as for understanding real systems.

Compile time binding fixes the physical address into the program before it ever runs, and it only works if the operating system can guarantee the program will always load at that one exact location, a rare and fairly old approach found in tiny, statically located systems. Load time binding waits until the program is actually loaded into memory, deciding the physical address at that point but before execution begins. Run time binding, the modern standard used by essentially every general purpose operating system today, defers the decision all the way until each individual memory access, translating it live through the MMU every single time, exactly as shown throughout this chapter.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408759737-569900605.png

{"headers":["Binding time","When it happens","How common today"],"rows":[["Compile time","The physical address is fixed into the program before it ever runs, only possible if the program is guaranteed to load at one exact location","Very rare, limited to tiny fixed purpose systems"],["Load time","The physical address is decided when the program is loaded into memory, but before it starts executing","Uncommon, used by some simple loaders"],["Run time","Every single memory access is translated live by the MMU while the program executes","The modern standard on essentially every general purpose operating system"]]}

This timing distinction, along with the full trade offs between the three, gets covered in complete depth in the dedicated Address Binding chapter. This chapter only needs you to recognize the three names and to know that run time binding through the MMU is what actually happens on the systems you use every day.
8. Logical vs Physical Address at a Glance
blocks.text: 8. Logical vs Physical Address at a Glance

blocks.content: With the mechanics established, it helps to line the two kinds of addresses up side by side and see the contrast in one place.

9. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle
A few misunderstandings show up again and again once this topic reaches practice, and they are worth naming directly.

["Assuming that a pointer value a program prints out is the real physical RAM address. It almost never is; it is a logical address, and the MMU translates it into a physical address later, on every access, invisibly to the program.","Believing translation happens once, at program startup, and the physical address then stays fixed for the whole run. In reality every single memory access is translated independently, every time, by the MMU.","Treating the limit register check as optional or as a software convention. It is enforced directly by hardware on every access, and it is the actual mechanism that keeps one program from touching another program's memory.","Confusing relocation, moving a program to a different physical location, with virtual memory, letting a program use more logical address space than physically exists. Relocation is the simple mechanism this chapter covers; virtual memory is a much larger idea built on top of it."]
items: Assuming that a pointer value a program prints out is the real physical RAM address. It almost never is; it is a logical address, and the MMU translates it into a physical address later, on every access, invisibly to the program.

Believing translation happens once, at program startup, and the physical address then stays fixed for the whole run. In reality every single memory access is translated independently, every time, by the MMU.

Treating the limit register check as optional or as a software convention. It is enforced directly by hardware on every access, and it is the actual mechanism that keeps one program from touching another program's memory.

Confusing relocation, moving a program to a different physical location, with virtual memory, letting a program use more logical address space than physically exists. Relocation is the simple mechanism this chapter covers; virtual memory is a much larger idea built on top of it.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain the MMU's role precisely: it sits between the CPU and RAM, it translates a logical address into a physical address on every single memory access using the base and limit registers, and it enforces protection by trapping any access beyond the limit. This exact explanation, stated cleanly, is one of the most commonly asked foundational operating systems interview questions.

Everything else in the Memory Management module rests on this one distinction. Paging and segmentation are simply more sophisticated ways of organizing the base and limit idea, and virtual memory is what happens when the logical address space is allowed to grow past what physical RAM alone could ever hold.
